label: Battle roll
summary: The plural form of another name of the game concept Battle Roll (the random rolls commanders make during a battle).
details: In a text, `[advantage_rolls|E]` shows "Advantage Rolls" linked to the explanation of battle rolls. The rolls go from 0 to 10 and are fully random. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Adventurer
summary: The game concept Adventurer: an unlanded character who leads a camp.
details: In a text, `[adventurer|E]` shows "Adventurer" linked to the concept's explanation. Adventurers have no vassals and no regular passive income; they earn by taking task contracts or calling in favors from their contacts. They roam the map freely and must keep enough provisions.

label: Camp
summary: Another name of the game concept Camp: the portable home (domicile) of an adventurer, which moves across the map with them.
details: In a text, `[adventurer_camp|E]` shows "Adventurer Camp" linked to the explanation of camps. Camp buildings built there give the adventurer bonuses in place of the counties a landed ruler would have. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Camp
summary: The plural form of another name of the game concept Camp (the portable homes of adventurers).
details: In a text, `[adventurer_camps|E]` shows "Adventurer Camps" linked to the explanation of camps. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Adventurer
summary: The icon form of the game concept Adventurer (an unlanded character who leads a camp).
details: `[adventurer_i]` shows the adventurer government icon instead of a word; with `|E` it is also linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla writes it at the start of perk effect lines for adventurers.

label: Adventurer
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Adventurer (an unlanded character who leads a camp).
details: In a text, `[adventurer_possessive|E]` shows "Adventurer's" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for example when speaking of an adventurer's wages in task contract texts.

label: Siege replenishment
summary: The game concept Siege Replenishment: when an adventurer wins a siege of a holding, part of their men-at-arms are refilled.
details: In a text, `[adventurer_siege_replenishment|E]` shows "Siege Replenishment" linked to the concept's explanation. Every men-at-arms regiment in the army is refilled by twice the holding's loot value. Vanilla uses it in an adventurer perk that doubles the effect.

label: Adventurer
summary: The plural form of the game concept Adventurer (unlanded characters who lead a camp).
details: In a text, `[adventurers|E]` shows "Adventurers" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for example to say that adventurers have followers instead of courtiers.

label: Adventurer
summary: The plural possessive form of the game concept Adventurer (unlanded characters who lead a camp).
details: In a text, `[adventurers_possessive|E]` shows "Adventurers'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Aftermath
summary: The game concept Aftermath: the phase of a battle after one side has won, when the winner hunts down as many retreating soldiers as they can.
details: In a text, `[aftermath|E]` shows "Aftermath" linked to the concept's explanation. Men-at-arms with high pursuit kill more soldiers in this phase, and those with high screen protect their own side's soldiers. Vanilla uses it to name the current combat phase.

label: Agents
summary: Another name of the game concept Agents: a character taking part in a scheme who helps it in one of three ways.
details: In a text, `[agent|E]` shows the word "Agent" linked to the explanation of agents. An agent can raise the success chance, change the scheme's speed, or improve its secrecy. Only the target's courtiers, guests and direct vassals can be recruited, and for hostile schemes agents close to the target matter most.

label: Agent discovery
summary: The game concept Agent Discovery: agents of a secret scheme who are found out may be treated as criminals by their liege.
details: In a text, `[agent_discovery|E]` shows "Agent Discovery" linked to the concept's explanation. If their liege sees them as criminals, discovered agents are likely to be imprisoned. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Agent discovery
summary: Another name of the game concept Agent Discovery: agents of a secret scheme who are found out may be treated as criminals by their liege.
details: In a text, `[agent_discovery_discovered|E]` shows the word "Discovered" linked to the explanation of agent discovery. Vanilla uses it in the secret scheme concept text (agents "have a chance of being Discovered").

label: Agents
summary: The icon form of the game concept Agents (characters taking part in a scheme to help it).
details: `[agent_i]` shows the scheme agent icon instead of a word; with `|E` it is also linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla writes it in the potential agents window before an agent's contribution.

label: Agents
summary: The game concept Agents: characters taking part in a scheme, each helping it in one of three ways.
details: In a text, `[agents|E]` shows "Agents" linked to the concept's explanation. An agent can raise the success chance, change the scheme's speed, or improve its secrecy. Only the target's courtiers, guests and direct vassals can be recruited.

label: Religious knowledge
summary: Another name of the game concept Religious Knowledge: which tenets and doctrines of other religious practices a character knows.
details: In a text, `[agnostic_knowledge|E]` shows the word "Knowledge" linked to the explanation of religious knowledge. All tenets and doctrines of your own faith are known; known ones from elsewhere can be used when founding a divergent rite or taken as personal tenets, and knowing all of a rite's makes conversion easier. Vanilla uses it when a character learns another rite's tenets and doctrines.

label: Cautious
summary: The game concept Cautious: an AI ruler personality that wants to be ready when someone declares war on them.
details: In a text, `[ai_cautious_personality|E]` shows "Cautious" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers avoid starting offensive wars and prefer a slow buildup, keep a reserve of gold for defense, and invest in buildings and men-at-arms.

label: Conqueror
summary: The game concept Conqueror: an AI ruler personality that wants to grow its realm through war at any cost.
details: In a text, `[ai_conqueror_personality|E]` shows "Conqueror" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers put all their gold into the war chest or men-at-arms, declare far more wars than usual, make unreliable allies, and skip pleasures like activities and inspirations.

label: Conqueror
summary: The plural form of the game concept Conqueror (AI rulers who want to grow their realm through war at any cost).
details: In a text, `[ai_conquerors_personality|E]` shows "Conquerors" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a game rule text about which characters become conquerors.

label: Builder
summary: The game concept Builder: an AI ruler personality that puts all its gold into developing the realm.
details: In a text, `[ai_economical_boom_personality|E]` shows "Builder" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers empty their treasury on buildings and men-at-arms, build more economic buildings and holdings, and only save gold when directly threatened, for example by a strong faction.

label: Unpredictable
summary: The game concept Unpredictable: an AI ruler personality whose traits push it toward no particular economic strategy.
details: In a text, `[ai_economical_unpredictable_personality|E]` shows "Unpredictable" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers may invest heavily in buildings for a while like a builder, or grow slowly with a gold reserve, and go to war at a normal pace.

label: Pious builder
summary: The game concept Pious Builder: an AI ruler personality that puts all its gold into gaining piety.
details: In a text, `[ai_pious_builder_personality|E]` shows "Pious Builder" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers spend on religious and ceremonial buildings, great projects, activities and decisions, build more pious buildings and temple holdings, and only save gold when directly threatened.

label: Warlike
summary: The game concept Warlike: an AI ruler personality that always wants to be ready to declare war.
details: In a text, `[ai_warlike_personality|E]` shows "Warlike" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers save gold for war before developing their realm; after a long peace they spend their war chest on buildings.

label: Aligned bloc member house
summary: Another name of the game concept Aligned Bloc Member House: a house in a house bloc that has the same house aspiration as the bloc's leading house.
details: In a text, `[aligned_bloc_house|E]` shows "Aligned Bloc House" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Aligned bloc member house
summary: The plural of another name of the game concept Aligned Bloc Member House (houses in a bloc that share the leading house's aspiration).
details: In a text, `[aligned_bloc_houses|E]` shows "Aligned Bloc Houses" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Aligned bloc member house
summary: The game concept Aligned Bloc Member House: a house that has joined a house bloc and has the same house aspiration as the bloc's leading house.
details: In a text, `[aligned_bloc_member_house|E]` shows "Aligned Bloc Member House" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the confederation window's cohesion lines for the heads of such houses.

label: Aligned bloc member house
summary: The plural form of the game concept Aligned Bloc Member House (houses in a bloc that share the leading house's aspiration).
details: In a text, `[aligned_bloc_member_houses|E]` shows "Aligned Bloc Member Houses" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Alliance
summary: The game concept Alliance: a diplomatic bond between two rulers.
details: In a text, `[alliance|E]` shows "Alliance" linked to the concept's explanation. Independent rulers can call their allies into their wars. Alliances come from and are kept by a marriage or betrothal, as long as the wed characters are closely enough related to the two rulers.

label: Alliance
summary: The plural form of the game concept Alliance (a diplomatic bond between two rulers).
details: In a text, `[alliances|E]` shows "Alliances" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for example in the AI personality texts about honoring alliances.

label: Alliance
summary: Another name of the game concept Alliance: a diplomatic bond between two rulers.
details: In a text, `[allied|E]` shows the word "Allied" linked to the explanation of alliances. Vanilla uses it in effect texts like "You are allowed to be allied with …".

label: Alliance
summary: Another name of the game concept Alliance: a diplomatic bond between two rulers.
details: In a text, `[allies|E]` shows the word "Allies" linked to the explanation of alliances. Vanilla uses it for example in war texts about allies sharing prestige.

label: Alliance
summary: Another name of the game concept Alliance: a diplomatic bond between two rulers.
details: In a text, `[ally|E]` shows the word "Ally" linked to the explanation of alliances. Vanilla uses it for example in "Attacking an ally".

label: Alliance
summary: The icon form of the game concept Alliance (a diplomatic bond between two rulers).
details: In a text, `[ally_i|E]` shows the alliance icon instead of a word, linked to the explanation of alliances. Vanilla uses it in the military strength comparison before the number of allies.

label: Court amenities
summary: Another name of the game concept Court Amenities: the standards of living a ruler sets for their royal court.
details: In a text, `[amenities|E]` shows the word "Amenities" linked to the explanation of court amenities. There are four categories (fashion, food, lodging, servants), each with several levels; spending more usually brings more court grandeur. Tribal rulers cannot choose the higher levels.

label: Ancestral claim
summary: The game concept Ancestral Claim: a casus belli (reason for war) to take all lands within a title you claim through a Legitimizing legend.
details: In a text, `[ancestral_claim|E]` shows "Ancestral Claim" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a legacy's effect text that grants access to this casus belli.

label: Anointment
summary: Another name of the game concept Anointment: a kind of coronation in which the ruler seeks the blessing of their head of faith (or the clergy head of rite when there is none).
details: In a text, `[anointment|E]` shows "Anointment" linked to the concept's explanation. In some faiths a ruler needs it to count as a legitimate ruler. The host secures the religious leader's support with the Request Anointment interaction.

label: Request anointment
summary: The game concept Request Anointment: a character interaction an empire-tier ruler or higher uses on their head of faith (or the clergy head of rite when there is none) to gain support for an anointment.
details: In a text, `[anointment_request|E]` shows "Request Anointment" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in coronation texts telling the player to secure that support.

label: Anointment
summary: The plural form of the game concept Anointment (a coronation blessed by the head of faith or head of rite).
details: In a text, `[anointments|E]` shows "Anointments" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it to note that anointments, unlike other coronations, may be held outside the host's realm.

label: Challenger head of faith
summary: Another name of the game concept Challenger Head of Faith: a rival head of faith raised against the one of the mainline rite.
details: In a text, `[antipope|E]` shows the word "Antipope" linked to the explanation of the challenger head of faith. A ruler can sponsor one of their clergy as challenger; a clergy ruler, or a ruler of a faith with a temporal head of faith, can declare themselves instead. Vanilla uses it in a situation catalyst text about a clergy member declaring themselves antipope.

label: Appointment succession law
summary: Another name of the game concept Appointment Succession Law: a succession in which the title and its holdings go to the candidate with the highest candidate score.
details: In a text, `[appointment|E]` shows the word "Appointment" linked to the explanation of appointment succession laws. Vanilla uses it in the succession result text ("Succession via Appointment …").

label: Appointment level
summary: The game concept Appointment Level: a requirement some appointment succession laws set before a character can be a candidate.
details: In a text, `[appointment_level|E]` shows "Appointment Level" linked to the concept's explanation. The level is measured in a particular currency, and each law can use a different one; higher-tier titles usually ask for a higher level.

label: Appointment level
summary: The plural form of the game concept Appointment Level (the candidate requirements some appointment succession laws set).
details: In a text, `[appointment_levels|E]` shows "Appointment Levels" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Prominence
summary: The game concept Prominence: how attractive a title is to the candidates who could be appointed to it.
details: In a text, `[appointment_prominence|E]` shows "Prominence" linked to the concept's explanation. A candidate who already holds a title is only appointed to another of the same tier if the new one has higher prominence. It mostly depends on local wealth and closeness to the realm capital.

label: Appointment succession law
summary: Another name of the game concept Appointment Succession Law: a succession in which the title and its holdings go to the candidate with the highest candidate score.
details: In a text, `[appointment_succession|E]` shows "Appointment Succession" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in an interaction text about a character not being eligible for it.

label: Appointment succession law
summary: The game concept Appointment Succession Law: a kind of succession law under which the title and its holdings go to the candidate with the highest candidate score.
details: In a text, `[appointment_succession_law|E]` shows "Appointment Succession Law" linked to the concept's explanation. The laws of this kind include appointment, acclamation and celestial appointment succession, among others.

label: Appointment succession law
summary: The plural form of the game concept Appointment Succession Law (the succession laws that give a title to the best-scoring candidate).
details: In a text, `[appointment_succession_laws|E]` shows "Appointment Succession Laws" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the appointment level concept text.

label: Appointment succession law
summary: Another plural name of the game concept Appointment Succession Law (successions that give a title to the best-scoring candidate).
details: In a text, `[appointments|E]` shows the word "Appointments" linked to the explanation of appointment succession laws. Vanilla uses it in an effect text saying a character cannot gain appointments for a while.

label: Aptitude
summary: The game concept Aptitude: how well a character performs in a role at court, such as a court position, diarch or tax collector.
details: In a text, `[aptitude|E]` shows "Aptitude" linked to the concept's explanation. It has 5 levels, from Terrible to Excellent, and the level decides the bonuses the liege gets from employing the character in that role.

label: Aptitude
summary: The icon form of the game concept Aptitude (how well a character performs in a court role).
details: `[aptitude_i]` shows the aptitude icon instead of a word; with `|E` it is also linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla writes it before aptitude values in council task texts.

label: Abbot
summary: The game concept Abbot: the ruler of a monastic holy order, who is also the head of rite of the rite the order champions.
details: In a text, `[archabbot|E]` shows the word "Abbot" linked to the concept's explanation. The abbot guides the order's members in study and in spreading its core tenets, and the order may have a patron who supports it with wealth and influence.

label: Archbishop
summary: The game concept Archbishop: the Christian holder of an archdiocese, a duchy-tier clerical title whose region can span several realms.
details: In a text, `[archbishop|E]` shows "Archbishop" linked to the concept's explanation. The archbishop stands above the bishops and lesser clergy of that region and answers to the head of faith.

label: Archbishop
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Archbishop (the Christian holder of an archdiocese).
details: In a text, `[archbishop_possessive|E]` shows "Archbishop's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Archbishop
summary: The plural form of the game concept Archbishop (the Christian holders of archdioceses).
details: In a text, `[archbishops|E]` shows "Archbishops" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for example in an important-action text about appointing archbishops as cardinals.

label: Archbishop
summary: The plural possessive form of the game concept Archbishop (the Christian holders of archdioceses).
details: In a text, `[archbishops_possessive|E]` shows "Archbishops'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Archdiocese
summary: The game concept Archdiocese: the Christian form of a clerical region, held by an archbishop and seated in a capital county.
details: In a text, `[archdiocese|E]` shows "Archdiocese" linked to the concept's explanation. A grand cathedral may be built in its seat. A Christian ruler answers in spiritual matters to the archbishop of the archdiocese that contains their capital county.

label: Archdiocese
summary: The plural form of the game concept Archdiocese (the Christian clerical regions held by archbishops).
details: In a text, `[archdioceses|E]` shows "Archdioceses" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a tutorial text saying Christian clerical regions are called archdioceses.

label: Archers
summary: The singular form of the game concept Archers: men-at-arms who fight on foot with ranged weapons.
details: In a text, `[archer|E]` shows "Archer" linked to the explanation of archers. Archers generally counter skirmishers and are countered by heavy and light cavalry. Vanilla uses it in an accolade text about fighting alongside archer men-at-arms.

label: Archer cavalry
summary: The game concept Archer Cavalry: mounted men-at-arms armed with ranged weapons.
details: In a text, `[archer_cavalry|E]` shows "Archer Cavalry" linked to the concept's explanation. They generally counter heavy infantry, are countered by crossbow archers, and are often strong on flat terrain, especially steppe.

label: Archers
summary: The game concept Archers: men-at-arms who fight on foot with ranged weapons.
details: In a text, `[archers|E]` shows "Archers" linked to the concept's explanation. Each kind differs, but archers generally counter skirmishers and are countered by heavy and light cavalry.

label: Army
summary: The plural form of the game concept Army (the forces used to fight battles and besiege holdings in wars).
details: In a text, `[armies|E]` shows "Armies" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for example in the army maintenance breakdown ("Raised Armies").

label: Army
summary: The game concept Army: a force used to win wars by fighting other armies and by besieging and occupying enemy fortified holdings.
details: In a text, `[army|E]` shows "Army" linked to the concept's explanation. Armies are raised at rally points and are made mostly of levies and men-at-arms, plus mercenaries and holy orders. They can cross water by paying gold for transport, and can lose soldiers to attrition.

label: Army commander
summary: The game concept Army Commander: the character leading an army.
details: In a text, `[army_commander|E]` shows "Army Commander" linked to the concept's explanation. Any courtier or direct vassal can be made commander, within limits of age, health and doctrines. In battle the commander's martial skill strongly affects the advantage, and while a commander is present extra rolls are made to raise it.

label: Army commander
summary: The plural form of the game concept Army Commander (the characters leading armies).
details: In a text, `[army_commanders|E]` shows "Army Commanders" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the martial skill concept text.

label: Artifact
summary: The game concept Artifact: a notable object that gives bonuses to the character using it.
details: In a text, `[artifact|E]` shows "Artifact" linked to the concept's explanation. Some artifacts are rarer than others. Like titles, characters can hold claims on an artifact and try to take it.

label: Artifact claim
summary: The game concept Artifact Claim: someone's rightful claim to an artifact.
details: In a text, `[artifact_claim|E]` shows "Artifact Claim" linked to the concept's explanation. With a claim on an artifact you do not have, you can take actions against it and its owner, such as a scheme to steal it back. There are personal claims for characters and house claims for houses.

label: Artifact claim
summary: The plural form of the game concept Artifact Claim (rightful claims to artifacts).
details: In a text, `[artifact_claims|E]` shows "Artifact Claims" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the artifact concept text.

label: Artifact durability
summary: The game concept Artifact Durability: how much wear an artifact can still take; when it runs out, the artifact is destroyed.
details: In a text, `[artifact_durability|E]` shows "Artifact Durability" linked to the concept's explanation. Durability drops over time and also in some events, such as sieges and successions. Reforging or repairing the artifact restores it. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Artifact
summary: The icon form of the game concept Artifact (a notable object that gives bonuses to its user).
details: In a text, `[artifact_i]` shows the artifact icon instead of a word. Vanilla puts it right before `[artifact|E]`, as in "Request an [artifact_i][artifact|E] as tribute".

label: Artifact rarity
summary: The game concept Artifact Rarity: how rare an artifact is.
details: In a text, `[artifact_rarity|E]` shows "Artifact Rarity" linked to the concept's explanation. The levels go from Common (the default, never shown) up through three higher levels, the highest being Illustrious. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Artifact
summary: The plural form of the game concept Artifact (notable objects that give bonuses to their users).
details: In a text, `[artifacts|E]` shows "Artifacts" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it for example in court position texts.

label: Asexual
summary: The game concept Asexual: a character who feels little or no attraction to anyone, whatever their gender.
details: In a text, `[asexual|E]` shows "Asexual" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a game rule effect about the chance of generated characters being asexual.

label: Mandala aspect
summary: Another name of the game concept Mandala Aspect: one of the divine aspects a mandala ruler aligns with to be revered as a god.
details: In a text, `[aspect|E]` shows the word "Aspect" linked to the explanation of mandala aspects. The aspects are Creation, Serenity, Destruction and Trickery, and the chosen one shapes what is expected of the ruler.

label: Aspect of creation
summary: The game concept Aspect of Creation: the mandala aspect that rewards economic and organizational work.
details: In a text, `[aspect_of_creation|E]` shows "Aspect of Creation" linked to the concept's explanation. It centers on stewardship: building in a row gives stacks of a modifier, and regular construction gives piety.

label: Aspect of destruction
summary: The game concept Aspect of Destruction: the mandala aspect that rewards ruling through fear and conquest.
details: In a text, `[aspect_of_destruction|E]` shows "Aspect of Destruction" linked to the concept's explanation. It centers on martial, gives military bonuses and the mandala plunder casus belli, and limits how the ruler may die.

label: Aspect of serenity
summary: The game concept Aspect of Serenity: the mandala aspect that rewards peace and diplomacy.
details: In a text, `[aspect_of_serenity|E]` shows "Aspect of Serenity" linked to the concept's explanation. It centers on diplomacy, and staying out of offensive wars gives stacks of a modifier.

label: Aspect of trickery
summary: The game concept Aspect of Trickery: the mandala aspect that rewards controlling others without them knowing.
details: In a text, `[aspect_of_trickery|E]` shows "Aspect of Trickery" linked to the concept's explanation. It centers on intrigue: the ruler can spend piety to bribe scheme agents and gets the leverage contribution scheme.

label: Mandala aspect
summary: The plural of another name of the game concept Mandala Aspect (the divine aspects a mandala ruler can align with).
details: In a text, `[aspects|E]` shows "Aspects" linked to the explanation of mandala aspects. Vanilla uses it in a scheme odds line ("You have differing Aspects").

label: House aspiration
summary: Another name of the game concept House Aspiration: the goals and methods a Japanese house follows, each giving its own bonuses and opportunities.
details: In a text, `[aspiration|E]` shows the word "Aspiration" linked to the explanation of house aspirations. The house head picks the aspiration and can spend prestige to commit further for stronger benefits. Vanilla uses it in the effect text for changing a house's aspiration.

label: House aspiration
summary: The plural of another name of the game concept House Aspiration (the goals and methods a Japanese house follows).
details: In a text, `[aspirations|E]` shows "Aspirations" linked to the explanation of house aspirations. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Master assassin
summary: Another name of the game concept Master Assassin: a court position available to faiths with the Fedayeen core tenet.
details: In a text, `[assassin|E]` shows the word "Assassin" linked to the explanation of the master assassin, a fanatic who works with lesser assassins to kill those seen as enemies of the faith. Vanilla lines like `[assassin.GetHerHim]` are a different thing: they use a saved character named `assassin`, not this concept.

label: Assault
summary: The game concept Assault: a besieging army storming a fortified holding, at the risk of losing many soldiers.
details: In a text, `[assault|E]` shows "Assault" linked to the concept's explanation. An assault is only possible once the holding's walls are breached, which needs siege weapons in the army.

label: Assault
summary: Another name of the game concept Assault: a besieging army storming a fortified holding.
details: In a text, `[assaulted|E]` shows the word "Assaulted" linked to the explanation of assaults. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Assault
summary: Another name of the game concept Assault: a besieging army storming a fortified holding.
details: In a text, `[assaulting|E]` shows the word "Assaulting" linked to the explanation of assaults. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: Assault
summary: The plural form of the game concept Assault (a besieging army storming a fortified holding).
details: In a text, `[assaults|E]` shows "Assaults" linked to the explanation of assaults. No vanilla text links it by this name.

label: At peace opinion
summary: The game concept At Peace Opinion: the opinion penalty that vassals of the same faith give a ruler who stays at peace too long, when the faith has the Warmonger tenet.
details: In a text, `[at_peace_opinion|E]` shows "At Peace Opinion" linked to the concept's explanation. It replaces the usual offensive war opinion penalty for that faith, and vassals of the same faith think less of a ruler who is at peace for too long.

label: At peace opinion
summary: A short name of the game concept At Peace Opinion (the penalty vassals of a Warmonger-tenet faith give a ruler who stays at peace too long).
details: In a text, `[at_peace_opinion_short|E]` shows "At Peace" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it as the label of that opinion in character relations.

label: Attraction
summary: Another name of the game concept Attraction: a kind of opinion that only affects characters whose sexuality matches your gender.
details: In a text, `[attracted|E]` shows the word "Attracted" linked to the explanation of attraction. Vanilla uses it in the sexuality concept text ("which other characters they are potentially attracted to").

label: Attraction
summary: The game concept Attraction: a kind of opinion that only affects characters whose sexuality matches your gender.
details: In a text, `[attraction|E]` shows "Attraction" linked to the concept's explanation. For example a homosexual man feels it toward other men, an asexual character toward no one. For women it stops having an effect above a certain age set in the game's defines.

label: Attrition
summary: The game concept of attrition: an army losing soldiers to desertion, sickness or hunger.
details: It happens when the army runs out of supplies, while it besieges a fortified holding, or when it moves from one hostile county into another that does not border a county it already controls. In a text, `[attrition|E]` shows the word Attrition, linked to the game's explanation of it. Vanilla uses it in tooltips about raiding and supply.

label: Attrition
summary: The icon of the attrition concept (an army losing soldiers to desertion, sickness or hunger).
details: `attrition_i` is another name of the Attrition concept whose text is just the attrition icon (`@attrition_icon!`), so `[attrition_i]` puts the icon into a text. Vanilla writes it without `|E`, right before a number, in the tooltip of the Kurultai task that organizes raiders.

label: Autonomous vassals crown authority
summary: The lowest level of crown authority, where vassals have no opinion penalty toward their liege and the liege has only basic power over them.
details: Crown authority is the realm law that sets how much power a ruler has over their vassals. `[autonomous_vassals|E]` shows the words Autonomous Vassals, linked to this concept's explanation; it is another name of the Autonomous Vassals Crown Authority concept. Vanilla uses it in the crown authority explanation that lists the four levels.

label: Autonomous vassals crown authority
summary: The lowest level of crown authority: vassals have no opinion penalty toward their liege, and the liege has only basic power over them.
details: `[autonomous_vassals_crown_authority|E]` in a text shows the full name Autonomous Vassals Crown Authority, linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a decision requirement that the player's liege has this law.

label: Available spouse
summary: A spouse who is free to take on the duties of the spouse's seat on a ruler's council.
details: Common reasons a spouse is not available: they rule their own realm, live at another ruler's court, are imprisoned, or have a trait such as Incapable. `[available_spouse|E]` shows the words Available Spouse, linked to this explanation. Vanilla uses it in the council's message that a ruler has no available spouse.

label: Banishment
summary: Banishment: sending an imprisoned character out of the realm, one of the harshest punishments.
details: A banished landed ruler loses their lands (is deposed); a banished courtier has their belongings seized. Banishing someone without a reason, such as a severe crime, counts as very tyrannical. `[banish|E]` shows the word Banish, linked to the Banishment concept; vanilla uses it among the punishments for crimes, in the banish reason explanation and in the interaction text `RELEASE_BANISH`.

label: Banishment reason
summary: A banishment reason: a right that lets a liege banish a certain subject from their dungeon freely.
details: Such reasons most often come from the subject being a criminal. `[banish_reason|E]` shows the words Banishment Reason, linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in effect texts about a character conceding their right to banish another.

label: Banishment reason
summary: Banishment reasons: rights that let a liege banish certain subjects from their dungeon freely, most often because they are criminals.
details: `[banish_reasons|E]` shows the plural Banishment Reasons, linked to the Banishment Reason concept. Vanilla uses it in a vassal interaction text about having crimes pardoned, which clears such reasons against you.

label: Banishment
summary: Banishment: an imprisoned character sent out of the realm as a harsh punishment.
details: Banished landed rulers are deposed and banished courtiers lose their belongings; banishing without a reason is very tyrannical. `[banished|E]` shows the word Banished, linked to the Banishment concept. Vanilla uses it in the banish effect's texts ("Is banished").

label: Banishment
summary: Banishment: sending an imprisoned character out of the realm, arguably the harshest punishment.
details: A banished ruler with land is deposed, a banished courtier has their assets seized, and banishing without a reason such as a severe crime is extremely tyrannical. `[banishment|E]` shows the word Banishment, linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name directly.

label: Bargain fealty
summary: A special interaction for struggle rulers defending in a war: the war leader asks a neighbouring higher-ranked ruler to join the war in return for becoming their vassal.
details: Only rulers involved in a struggle can use it. `[bargain_fealty|E]` shows the words Bargain Fealty, linked to the explanation. Vanilla uses it in a struggle parameter that unlocks the interaction and in tooltips saying it cannot be used over a border raid or a struggle conquest.

label: Bargain fealty
summary: Bargain fealty: a struggle ruler at war in defence gains a higher-ranked neighbour's help by becoming their vassal.
details: `[bargained_fealty|E]` shows the words Bargained Fealty, linked to the Bargain Fealty concept. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Baron
summary: A ruler whose primary title is a barony, the lowest rank, just below counts.
details: A baron cannot have vassals, and any ruler of higher rank can be their liege. `[baron|E]` shows the word Baron, linked to the concept's explanation; vanilla uses it in the list of ranks and in concept texts that limit something to landless characters and barons, such as the acclaimed knight.

label: Barony
summary: Baronies: titles of the lowest tier, the smallest pieces of land on the map.
details: Baronies are grouped into counties, and a barony that contains a holding always has a holder. `[baronies|E]` shows the plural Baronies, linked to the Barony concept. Vanilla uses it in explanations of leasing, counties and buildings.

label: Baron
summary: Barons: rulers whose primary title is a barony, the lowest rank.
details: They cannot have vassals, and any ruler above them in rank can be their liege. `[barons|E]` shows the plural Barons, linked to the Baron concept; vanilla uses it in the count explanation and in knight permission texts.

label: Barony
summary: A barony: a title of the lowest tier, the smallest area on the map.
details: Baronies make up counties, and a barony title with a holding in it must always have a holder. `[barony|E]` shows the word Barony, linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it widely, for example in building and achievement texts.

label: Barter
summary: Bartering: rulers of the Wanua government raise armies as barterers to gain gold from holdings peacefully.
details: It works like raiding but is not a hostile action, and it needs barter goods: 2 barter goods earn 1 loot from a holding, and with too few nothing happens. The holding bartered with gets a modifier, during which it cannot be looted or bartered with again. `[barter|E]` shows the word Barter, linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Barter goods
summary: Barter goods: island wares such as dried fish or rattan crafts that Wanua rulers use to barter and to keep up their armies.
details: They are produced by certain buildings, among them the building `tribe_01`. `[barter_goods|E]` shows the words Barter Goods, linked to the explanation. Vanilla uses it in the barter goods balance tooltip (with the change per month) and among a government's obligations.

label: Barter goods
summary: The icon of barter goods, the island wares Wanua rulers use to barter and to keep up their armies.
details: `barter_goods_i` is another name of the Barter Goods concept whose text is just its icon (`@barter_goods_icon!`). Vanilla writes `[barter_goods_i]` before an amount to show costs in barter goods (for example army maintenance and reinforcement).

label: Barter
summary: The icon of bartering, the peaceful raiding of Wanua rulers.
details: `barter_i` is another name of the Barter concept whose text is just the barter icon (`@barter_icon!`), so `[barter_i]` puts that icon into a text. No vanilla text uses it.

label: Barter
summary: Bartering: Wanua rulers gaining gold from holdings through their barterer armies, without hostility.
details: `[bartered|E]` shows the word Bartered, linked to the Barter concept. Vanilla uses it in messages that a barter is done and in the modifier text saying a recently bartered holding cannot be looted or bartered with until it expires.

label: Barterer
summary: A barterer: an army raised by a Wanua ruler to barter, which works like raiders but is not hostile to the holder of the holding it targets.
details: Raiding armies of other rulers can fight barterers and steal their loot. `[barterer|E]` shows the word Barterer, linked to the explanation. In message texts, `[barterer.GetShortUIName]` is something else: a character the message saved under the name `barterer`.

label: Barterer
summary: Barterers: armies raised by Wanua rulers to barter, not hostile to the holder of the holding they target.
details: Other rulers' raiding armies can fight them and take their loot. `[barterers|E]` shows the plural Barterers, linked to the Barterer concept; vanilla uses it in the barter explanation and in message filters about loot.

label: Barter
summary: Bartering: peaceful raiding by Wanua rulers, whose armies gain gold from holdings using barter goods.
details: `[bartering|E]` shows the word Bartering, linked to the Barter concept. Vanilla uses it in the loot explanation, in the government text that enables bartering, and in the message that a bartering army came back with loot.

label: Barter
summary: Bartering: Wanua rulers' armies gaining gold from holdings without being hostile.
details: `[barters|E]` shows the word Barters, linked to the Barter concept. Vanilla uses it in the message filter for an army that successfully barters with a holding.

label: Bastard
summary: A bastard: a child born outside marriage, who cannot inherit titles.
details: The parents can legitimize the child if their house head approves. Which house a bastard belongs to depends on the doctrines of the parents' faiths at birth. A bastard who is given titles or has children founds a new dynasty. `[bastard|E]` shows the word Bastard, linked to the explanation.

label: Bastard
summary: Bastards: children born outside marriage, barred from inheriting titles.
details: They can be legitimized with the house head's approval, and if they get titles or children they found a new dynasty. `[bastards|E]` shows the plural Bastards, linked to the Bastard concept; vanilla uses it in explanations of marriage, the house head and legitimacy.

label: Bastard
summary: Bastardy: being a child born outside marriage, which bars inheriting titles.
details: `[bastardy|E]` shows the word Bastardy, linked to the Bastard concept. Vanilla uses it once, in the list of things that affect a ruler's legitimacy.

label: Battle
summary: A battle: the fight that starts when two opposing armies enter the same barony.
details: One side often starts with an advantage from terrain, its commander and the commander's traits. Armies lose soldiers by the damage they take, and when one side has no soldiers left the battle moves to its aftermath; the winner gains war score. `[battle|E]` shows the word Battle, linked to the explanation, and vanilla uses it in many combat texts.

label: Battle advantage
summary: Battle advantage: what makes one side in a battle do more damage; the higher it is, the more damage its soldiers do.
details: A battle often starts with one side ahead because of terrain and the commander's martial skill and commander traits; both sides can gain more from their commander's rolls. `[battle_advantage|E]` shows the words Battle Advantage, linked to the explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Battle
summary: Battles: the fights that start when two opposing armies enter the same barony.
details: Advantage, casualties by damage taken and war score for the winner are part of the concept. `[battles|E]` shows the plural Battles, linked to the Battle concept; vanilla uses it in court position and other texts about winning or fighting battles.

label: Personality
summary: A character's personality: how they act toward you and others, set mainly by their personality traits.
details: Some modifiers and special traits, such as Conqueror, can also change how rulers behave. `[behave|E]` shows the word Behave, linked to the Personality concept; vanilla uses it in the AI personality tooltips.

label: Beneficiary
summary: Beneficiaries: dynasty members whom participants in a great holy war pick to receive land if the war is won.
details: Each beneficiary gets land in the target realm in proportion to their patron ruler's war contribution, and the largest contributor can make theirs take the main title fought over. `[beneficiaries|E]` shows the plural Beneficiaries, linked to the Beneficiary concept. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Beneficiary
summary: A beneficiary: the member of their dynasty whom a participant in a great holy war picks to receive land on victory.
details: How much land depends on the patron ruler's war contribution; the largest contributor can force their beneficiary to receive the main title being fought over. `[beneficiary|E]` shows the word Beneficiary, linked to the explanation; vanilla uses it in effect texts that select or remove a beneficiary.

label: Siege
summary: A siege: an army surrounding a fortified holding to starve it out, so that it can be occupied.
details: A siege starts by itself when an army that outnumbers the garrison enters a hostile fortified holding's location and stays there. Once the walls are breached, the army can assault the holding. `[besiege|E]` shows the word Besiege, linked to the Siege concept; vanilla uses it in army order texts ("Moving to besiege ...").

label: Siege
summary: A siege: an army surrounding a fortified holding to make it give up, so it can be occupied.
details: `[besieged|E]` shows the word Besieged, linked to the Siege concept. Vanilla uses it in the explanations of fort level and the garrison, which protects a holding from being besieged by small armies.

label: Siege
summary: A siege: an army starving out a fortified holding so it can be occupied.
details: `[besieging|E]` shows the word Besieging, linked to the Siege concept. Vanilla uses it in the assault explanation and in the siege window's soldier counts.

label: Best friend
summary: A best friend: a relation of lifelong dedication and support, stronger than a friend.
details: A character can have only one best friend. `[best_friend|E]` shows the words Best Friend, linked to the explanation; vanilla uses it in council task and other texts.

label: Best friend
summary: The possessive form of best friend, the relation of lifelong dedication that is stronger than friendship.
details: `[best_friend_possessive|E]` shows the words Best Friend's, linked to the Best Friend concept. Vanilla uses it in a cultural tradition about drawing on your best friend's education.

label: Best friend
summary: Best friends: characters bound by a relation of lifelong dedication, stronger than friendship.
details: Each character can have only one best friend. `[best_friends|E]` shows the words Best Friends, linked to the Best Friend concept; vanilla uses it in the friend explanation and in an interaction rule about hooks gained from being best friends.

label: Best friend
summary: The plural possessive of best friend, the relation of lifelong dedication and support.
details: `[best_friends_possessive|E]` shows the words Best Friends', linked to the Best Friend concept. No vanilla text uses it.

label: Bestow royal favor
summary: A councillor task of the chancellor that makes a chosen vassal in the realm think better of their liege.
details: The concept's name is the task's own name, Bestow Royal Favor. `[bestow_royal_favor|E]` shows it, linked to the explanation. Vanilla uses it where a royal court level unlocks the task and in a dynasty legacy that makes it more effective.

label: Betrothal
summary: A betrothal: a promise that two characters will marry later, made when one of them is not yet an adult.
details: Like a marriage it can bring an alliance, but it is easily broken, and it becomes a real marriage when they come of age. With the Tours and Tournaments content, a betrothal can also come from a promised grand wedding, and that kind becomes a marriage when the wedding is held; the game picks the description by that content. `[betrothal|E]` shows the word Betrothal, linked to the explanation.

label: Betrothal
summary: Betrothals: promises of a future marriage, made while one of the two is not yet an adult.
details: `[betrothals|E]` shows the plural Betrothals, linked to the Betrothal concept. Vanilla uses it in the marriage explanation and the tutorial.

label: Betrothal
summary: Betrothal: being promised in a future marriage.
details: A betrothal can bring an alliance, is easily broken, and turns into a marriage at adulthood. `[betrothed|E]` shows the word Betrothed, linked to the Betrothal concept; vanilla uses it in the texts of the effects that create a betrothal ("Becomes betrothed to ...").

label: Bisexual
summary: Bisexual: a character attracted to people of either the same or the opposite gender.
details: `[bisexual|E]` shows the word Bisexual, linked to the explanation. Vanilla uses it in the texts of the effect that sets the chance of generated characters being bisexual.

label: Bishop
summary: A bishop: a clergy member of a Christian faith who holds or leases temple holdings.
details: A bishop lives in an archdiocese and answers to its archbishop. One without land of their own but with leased titles serves under a secular liege; one with their own land can rule as an ecclesiastical ruler. `[bishop|E]` shows the word Bishop, linked to the explanation. In event texts, `[bishop.GetSheHe]` and the like are something else: a character the event saved under the name `bishop`.

label: Bishop
summary: The possessive form of bishop, a Christian clergy member who holds or leases temple holdings.
details: `[bishop_possessive|E]` shows the word Bishop's, linked to the Bishop concept. Vanilla uses it once, in a puppet action text about pressing a weak claim.

label: Bishop
summary: Bishops: Christian clergy members who hold or lease temple holdings.
details: They answer to the archbishop of their archdiocese. `[bishops|E]` shows the plural Bishops, linked to the Bishop concept; vanilla uses it in the ecclesiastical concept texts.

label: Bishop
summary: The plural possessive of bishop, a Christian clergy member holding or leasing temple holdings.
details: `[bishops_possessive|E]` shows the word Bishops', linked to the Bishop concept. No vanilla text uses it.

label: Blackmail
summary: Blackmail: using a criminal secret you know about a character, through an interaction, to try to gain a hook on them.
details: How strong the hook is depends on how severe the secret is, which often depends on faith doctrines. `[blackmail|E]` shows the word Blackmail, linked to the explanation; vanilla uses it in AI personality texts.

label: Blackmail
summary: Blackmail: gaining a hook on a character by threatening to reveal their criminal secret.
details: `[blackmailed|E]` shows the word Blackmailed, linked to the Blackmail concept. Vanilla uses it in the hook explanation and in a situation catalyst about a censor blackmailing a governor.

label: Blackmail
summary: Blackmail: using a known criminal secret of a character to try to gain a hook on them.
details: `[blackmailing|E]` shows the word Blackmailing, linked to the Blackmail concept. Vanilla uses it once, in a story about confronting infidelity.

label: House bloc
summary: A house bloc: a defensive alliance of houses within a realm, whose members all defend any member house that is attacked.
details: House heads decide whether to join, and the ruling members of their house in the realm follow them. A bloc always has a leading house, whose head can expel members and is the favoured ceremonial regent of all members. `[bloc|E]` shows the word Bloc, linked to the House Bloc concept; vanilla uses it often, for example in a decision about bloc cohesion.

label: Bloc cohesion
summary: Bloc cohesion: how united a house bloc is, with higher levels giving its member houses more benefits.
details: Which benefits depends on the leading house's house aspiration. Cohesion comes mainly from house relations between the members, which can raise or lower it; a large bloc or members with mismatched aspirations or governments lower it. `[bloc_cohesion|E]` shows the words Bloc Cohesion, linked to the explanation.

label: Bloc expansion war
summary: A bloc expansion war: a special war waged by a member of a house bloc.
details: The winner may appoint a ruler to the contested titles or keep them. Appointing someone gives the winner a hook on them, adds them to the winner's bloc, and founds a new house if they are not a house head. `[bloc_expansion|E]` shows the words Bloc Expansion, linked to the Bloc Expansion War concept; vanilla uses it in war names and advice texts.

label: Bloc expansion war
summary: A bloc expansion war: a special war waged by a member of a house bloc, after which the winner may install a ruler in the contested titles or keep them.
details: An installed ruler owes the winner a hook, joins the winner's bloc, and founds a new house if they are not a house head. `[bloc_expansion_war|E]` shows the words Bloc Expansion War, linked to the explanation; vanilla uses it in a message about winning such a war.

label: Bloc member house
summary: A bloc member house: any house that has joined a house bloc, its leading house included.
details: `[bloc_house|E]` shows the words Bloc House, linked to the Bloc Member House concept. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Bloc member house
summary: Bloc member houses: the houses that have joined a house bloc, including the leading one.
details: `[bloc_houses|E]` shows the words Bloc Houses, linked to the Bloc Member House concept. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Leading house
summary: The leading house: the house that all members of a house bloc agree to follow.
details: `[bloc_leader|E]` shows the words Bloc Leader, linked to the Leading House concept. In event texts, `[bloc_leader.GetHouse.GetBaseName]` and the like are something else: a character the event saved under the name `bloc_leader`.

label: Leading house
summary: The leading house: the agreed leader among the houses of a house bloc.
details: `[bloc_leadership|E]` shows the words Bloc Leadership, linked to the Leading House concept. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Bloc member house
summary: A bloc member house: a house that has joined a house bloc, which counts the leading house too.
details: `[bloc_member_house|E]` shows the words Bloc Member House, linked to the explanation. Vanilla uses it in the bloc tooltips of the confederation window.
